tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: drops and horizontal launches
tasks.focus: Start with zero vertical launch velocity; solve time, range and impact.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls horizontally at 6.00 m/s from a 7.35 m ledge. Find flight time, range, and impact speed and direction.
A projectile launches horizontally and lands 44.1 m below launch, 54.0 m away. Find launch speed and explain whether doubling this speed changes the fall time.

marking.point: The future root is t = 3.00 s.
Doubling uₓ does not change vertical conditions, so time stays 3.00 s.
Range doubles to 108 m in this no-drag model.

mastery.prompt: A horizontal launch from a greater height, with uₓ fixed, has…
mastery.why: t = √(2H/g), so increasing H increases the fall time.
Released from rest means initial velocity zero; gravity then changes it.

mastery.prompt: Two balls have equal vertical starting conditions but different uₓ. Their fall times are…
mastery.why: The vertical motion determines the shared fall time.

mastery.prompt: For vₓ = 8 and vᵧ = −9.8 m/s the impact speed is…
mastery.why: The components are perpendicular: √(8² + 9.8²) ≈ 12.7 m/s.

tasks.title: Projectile motion: equal-height launches — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: equal-height launches
tasks.focus: Launch and landing share a height; learn symmetry, flight time and range.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 18.0 m/s at 45.0° and lands at launch height. Find time to apex, total flight time, maximum height and range.

marking.point: Maximum height = uᵧ²/(2g) = 8.27 m above launch.

questions.prompt: A launcher has fixed speed 12.0 m/s. Can it reach a target 16.0 m away at launch height? Justify without guessing angles.

marking.point: Equal-height range is R = u² sin2θ/g.
Its maximum occurs at sin2θ = 1, θ = 45°.
The required 16.0 m exceeds this maximum, so no launch angle reaches the target under the model.

mastery.prompt: For equal launch and landing heights, total flight time is…
mastery.why: The rise and return take equal times; uᵧ/g is time to apex.

mastery.prompt: At equal-height landing, the speed without drag is…
mastery.why: Gravitational potential energy is unchanged between the endpoints.

options: range at equal heights and fixed speed
mastery.why: The range contains sin2θ; time and height depend on the vertical component.

options: equal heights, fixed speed, constant g and no drag
mastery.why: The maximum follows from sin2θ = 1 under the stated assumptions.

tasks.title: Projectile motion: unequal heights and impact — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: unequal heights and impact
tasks.focus: Land below or above launch; solve the quadratic and identify the physical event.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 12.0 m/s at 30.0° above horizontal from a 6.00 m platform. Find time to ground, range and impact speed.

marking.point: Select future root t = 1.88 s; discard the negative root.
Impact speed from v² = u² + 2gH is √261.6 = 16.2 m/s.

questions.prompt: A projectile has uₓ = 9.00 m/s and uᵧ = 12.0 m/s. Find both times it reaches 3.00 m above launch and the corresponding x-positions. Explain why height alone does not identify a target hit.

marking.point: Quadratic roots t = 0.283 s and 2.17 s.
The smaller root is rising; the larger root is falling, as vᵧ = 12.0 − 9.80t changes sign.
A target must match both x and y at the same time.

mastery.prompt: Landing 10 m below launch has Δy, with up positive,…
mastery.why: Δy is final minus initial height.

mastery.prompt: Two positive roots for an upward launch reaching a higher height describe…
mastery.why: The same reachable height can be crossed twice.
There is no real time satisfying the height condition.

mastery.prompt: At a lower landing the speed is…
options: greater than launch speed in the no-drag model
mastery.why: Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

tasks.title: Projectile motion: walls, targets and unknown launches — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: walls, targets and unknown launches
tasks.focus: Choose the event; work backwards from a target and combine coordinates.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 18.0 m/s at 35.0°. A wall 15.0 m away is 3.00 m above launch. Determine its clearance above the wall.

marking.point: Clearance = y − 3.00 = 2.43 m, so the ideal point projectile clears it.

questions.prompt: At a fixed launch angle of 45.0°, what speed reaches a target 12.0 m horizontally away and 2.00 m above launch? Explain the positivity condition in your rearrangement.

marking.point: Xtanθ − Y = 12.0 − 2.00 = 10.0 m > 0, so a physical solution exists.

mastery.prompt: To test clearance at a known wall x-position, find time using…
mastery.why: The wall is an intermediate event at a specified x.

mastery.prompt: A rim at 3.05 m and release at 1.80 m requires Δy =…
mastery.why: Target displacement is final minus initial height.
The object and target must coincide at the same event.

mastery.prompt: A faster target ahead moving in the same direction is…
options: not caught in the ideal constant-uₓ model
mastery.why: The horizontal gap does not close.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: beams, cantilevers and tipping — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Equilibrium: beams, cantilevers and tipping
tasks.focus: Draw the forces, choose a pivot, and calculate support forces and turning effects.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Structures are rigid and stationary; state support assumptions. Anticlockwise torque is positive.

questions.prompt: A uniform 5.00 m beam weighs 160 N and rests on end supports A and B. A 250 N point load acts 4.00 m from A. Find both support reactions.

marking.point: Beam weight acts 2.50 m from A.
Vertical balance: Rₐ + 280 = 410 gives Rₐ = 130 N upward.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m beam weighing 200 N rests on unbolted supports at x = 0 and x = 4.00 m. A 600 N person walks onto the overhang. Find the position x where tipping begins.

marking.point: At impending tipping the x = 0 support reaction is zero.
Take moments about the support at x = 4.00 m.
x = 4.00 + 200/600 = 4.33 m from the left end.
Further motion would require a downward reaction at the unbolted left support, so two-contact equilibrium fails.

mastery.prompt: Taking moments about A removes Rₐ because…
mastery.why: Its line of action passes through the pivot.

mastery.prompt: A uniform beam weight acts at…
mastery.why: Uniform mass distribution puts its centre of mass halfway along.

mastery.prompt: Two supports share a load equally when…
options: the complete load and geometry are symmetric
mastery.why: Force balance alone gives the total, while symmetry and moment balance give equal sharing.

mastery.prompt: A fixed cantilever support must usually supply…
options: a force and a reaction moment
mastery.why: The clamp balances both net force and net torque.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: ladders, friction and slipping — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Equilibrium: ladders, friction and slipping
tasks.focus: Resolve contact forces, use moment geometry and test friction limits.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Uniform rigid ladder; smooth vertical wall and rough horizontal floor unless stated. Anticlockwise torque positive.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m ladder weighs 180 N and leans at 65.0° to a rough floor against a smooth wall. Find the wall normal, floor normal and minimum floor friction coefficient.

marking.point: The smooth wall exerts only a horizontal normal.
Nwall = 42.0 N; horizontal balance gives the same required floor friction.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m ladder weighs 180 N and leans at 60.0° against a smooth wall. A 600 N person stands 4.00 m along it. With floor μs = 0.300, can it remain still?

marking.point: Required Nwall and floor friction = 283 N.
Required friction exceeds 234 N, so the assumed static position cannot hold.

options: a horizontal normal only in this model
mastery.why: The normal is perpendicular to the wall; smooth neglects friction.

mastery.prompt: For vertical weight at distance s along a ladder, the arm is…
mastery.why: The perpendicular distance is the horizontal projection.
Below the limit it adjusts to the required value.

mastery.prompt: Climbing higher generally makes required floor friction…
mastery.why: The person weight has a larger turning arm about the foot.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: signs, cables and angled supports — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Equilibrium: signs, cables and angled supports
tasks.focus: Balance angled tensions and combine force balance with hinge moments.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Cables are light and taut; hinges are frictionless; beams are rigid. Angles are measured from horizontal unless stated.

questions.prompt: A 240 N sign hangs from two equal cables, each 45.0° above horizontal. Find each cable tension and show why it is not 120 N.

marking.point: Symmetry and horizontal balance give equal tensions T.
120 N is each cable’s vertical component, not its total tension.

questions.prompt: A uniform horizontal 4.00 m beam weighs 160 N and supports a 240 N sign at its end. An end cable pulls up-left at 60.0°. Find cable tension and both hinge components.

marking.point: The horizontal cable component has zero moment about the hinge but enters horizontal force balance.

mastery.prompt: An angled cable’s vertical component, angle above horizontal, is…
mastery.why: The vertical side is opposite the angle.
Their horizontal components must cancel while vertical components support the weight.

mastery.prompt: For a horizontal beam, the cable horizontal component has torque about its hinge…
options: zero if its line passes through the hinge
mastery.why: The perpendicular lever arm is zero.

mastery.prompt: A cable strength rating should be compared with…
mastery.why: The cable carries the full tensile force.

tasks.title: Relativity: clocks, spacecraft and particle lifetimes — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Relativity: clocks, spacecraft and particle lifetimes
tasks.focus: Identify proper time and proper length; reconcile approaching, receding and particle scenarios.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Frames move inertially at constant relative velocity unless stated. β = |v|/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β²).

questions.prompt: A ship with proper longitudinal length 250 m moves at 0.800c relative to Earth. Two events occur at one onboard clock location 6.00 s apart according to that clock. Find Earth-measured length and interval.

marking.point: 6.00 s is proper time because both events are colocated on the onboard clock.
Only the dimension parallel to the relative motion contracts.

questions.prompt: A particle has proper mean lifetime 2.00 μs and travels at 0.600c in the laboratory. Find its mean laboratory travel distance and the equivalent detector travel distance in its rest frame.

marking.point: 0.600c × proper lifetime 2.00 μs also gives 360 m, reconciling the frames.

mastery.prompt: Proper time is measured between events…
options: at the same position in the clock rest frame
mastery.why: A clock present at both events records their proper interval.

mastery.prompt: Changing v from +0.80c to −0.80c changes γ…
mastery.why: The Lorentz factor depends on v².

mastery.prompt: A proper length 120 m at 0.80c along its length is measured…

tasks.title: Relativity extension: approaching, receding and overtaking — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Relativity extension: approaching, receding and overtaking
tasks.focus: Use signed velocities and distinguish a frame measurement from a closing rate.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Extension beyond the assessed 2026 velocity-transformation equations. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. One-dimensional inertial frames; +x to the right.

questions.prompt: Extension: A travels at +0.80c and B at −0.30c in Earth frame, with A initially left of B. Find A’s signed velocity measured by B and distinguish it from Earth’s closing rate.

marking.point: The closing rate is a separation rate in Earth coordinates; it is not B’s measured object speed.

questions.prompt: Extension: A ship moves at +0.50c relative to Earth. A probe moves backwards at −0.80c relative to the ship. Find its Earth velocity and interpret its sign.

marking.point: Transform from ship to Earth: u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²).
Unlike some backward ship-frame launches, this probe also moves backwards in Earth frame; the sign follows the calculation.

mastery.prompt: The inverse transformation expects u and v to be measured…
mastery.why: u is the object and v the observer velocity in S.

mastery.prompt: Two ships each at 0.60c approach in Earth frame. One measures the other’s speed as…
mastery.why: 1.20/1.36 = 0.882; 1.20c is the Earth-coordinate closing rate.

options: motion in the negative chosen direction
mastery.why: Velocity carries direction; speed is its magnitude.

tasks.title: Physics foundations: rearranging and testing equations — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Physics foundations: rearranging and testing equations
tasks.focus: Isolate the unknown, handle squared quantities and check dimensions.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both fresh written questions before revealing the marking guide. Explain equation choices and show units, signs and labelled diagrams where useful. Complete the four concept checks, review written working and record an improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use SI units, keep guard digits, and report units and direction where appropriate. Original exam-style questions unless a source is identified.

questions.prompt: A 3.00 kg object has kinetic energy 150 J. Rearrange for speed, then predict its speed if the energy increases to 600 J at the same mass.

marking.point: Energy increases by a factor of four, so speed increases by a factor of two.

questions.prompt: A 0.300 kg sample absorbs 18 000 J and rises through 50.0 K without phase change. Rearrange Q = mcΔT for c, calculate it, and check the units.

marking.point: c = Q/(mΔT), dividing by the complete product.
The denominator has units kg·K, so Q divided by it has the required specific-heat units.

mastery.why: Divide by the entire product mc.
Undo the square with a square root.
Energy is kg·m²/s² and division cancels kg.

mastery.prompt: Doubling speed at fixed mass changes Eₖ by…
mastery.why: Kinetic energy is proportional to v².

marking.point: Report (4.00 ± 0.12) m/s under the stated method.

questions.prompt: An empty balance reads +0.015 kg and a loaded balance reads 0.615 kg. Find corrected sample mass. Explain whether repeating the uncorrected reading fixes the error and distinguish precision from accuracy.

marking.point: Repeating and averaging the same offset does not remove it.
Precision concerns the spread of repeated measurements.
Accuracy concerns closeness to the reference or true value; calibration corrects this systematic offset.

mastery.prompt: For a difference, this method combines independent reading uncertainties by…
mastery.why: The central subtraction does not subtract uncertainty ranges.
Vertical units m divided by horizontal units s.

tasks.lessonTitle: Heating: temperature changes, heaters and efficiency
tasks.focus: Use Q = mcΔT and distinguish useful heating from source energy.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both fresh written questions before revealing the marking guide. Explain equation choices and show units, signs and labelled diagrams where useful. tasks.constants: Water c = 4180 J/(kg·K) unless stated. No phase change in Q = mcΔT calculations. Values supplied in each question override these defaults.

questions.prompt: A 0.400 kg water sample warms from 20.0°C to 70.0°C using a 1000 W input heater at 80.0% efficiency. Find useful heating energy, input energy and heating time.

marking.point: No phase change is assumed and efficiency accounts for input not reaching useful water heating.

questions.prompt: A 0.250 kg metal sample gains 3750 J while warming from 20.0°C to 50.0°C. Find c, then its signed energy change as it cools from 50.0°C to 10.0°C.

marking.point: It releases 5.00 kJ; the sample's energy change is negative.

mastery.prompt: At fixed mass and ΔT, a larger c requires…
mastery.why: Q = mcΔT.
Offsets cancel in differences.

mastery.prompt: During cooling, energy gained by the sample is…
mastery.why: ΔT is negative and ΔU = mcΔT.

mastery.prompt: A heater’s input Pt equals useful water heating…
options: only when all that input goes to the water
mastery.why: Other energy transfers require separate accounting.

tasks.title: Heating: melting, boiling and multistage energy — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Heating: melting, boiling and multistage energy
tasks.focus: Separate warming from changing state; calculate how much melts or boils.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both fresh written questions before revealing the marking guide. Explain equation choices and show units, signs and labelled diagrams where useful. Complete the four concept checks, review written working and record an improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use water c = 4180 J/(kg·K), ice c = 2100 J/(kg·K), fusion Lf = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and vaporisation Lv = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg unless stated. Water phase temperatures assume ordinary atmospheric pressure.

questions.prompt: Calculate energy to turn 0.0500 kg ice at −20.0°C into water at 30.0°C. Use the stated thermal constants and neglect losses.

marking.point: Distinct state and phase-change terms are required; one mcΔT term is insufficient.

questions.prompt: 0.120 kg ice at 0°C absorbs 20 040 J. Calculate melted mass, remaining ice mass and final temperature.

marking.point: Energy to melt all ice = 0.120 × 334 000 = 40 080 J, greater than available.
The ideal ice-water mixture remains at 0°C while both phases coexist.

mastery.prompt: During ideal melting at constant temperature, internal energy…
mastery.why: Latent energy changes microscopic arrangement and potential energy.
It is phase-change energy per mass.

mastery.prompt: If energy is insufficient to melt all the ice at 0°C, final state is…
options: ice and water at 0°C in the ideal model
mastery.why: Calculate the melted amount using Q/L.

mastery.prompt: To heat ice below 0°C into warm liquid, use…
options: one water c over the whole interval
ice warming + latent term + water warming
mastery.why: Each state and phase transition needs its own term.

tasks.constants: Use water c = 4180 J/(kg·K), ice Lf = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg unless stated. Assume insulated systems and negligible container heat capacity only where explicitly stated.

questions.prompt: In an insulated negligible-capacity cup, 0.200 kg water at 70.0°C mixes with 0.300 kg water at 20.0°C. Find final temperature and energy transferred.
Add 0.0400 kg ice at 0°C to 0.200 kg water at 25.0°C in an insulated negligible-capacity cup. Test whether all ice melts, then find final temperature.

marking.point: Cooling water to 0°C would release 0.200 × 4180 × 25.0 = 20 900 J.
Melting all ice needs 0.0400 × 334 000 = 13 360 J, so complete melting is possible.
The positive final temperature supports the assumed final all-liquid state.

mastery.prompt: Ideal equilibrium for two parts means…
mastery.why: Temperature equalises; internal energy depends on amounts and materials.

mastery.prompt: A simple mean of initial temperatures is justified when…
options: heat capacities are equal under the no-phase-change assumptions
mastery.why: The energy balance weights by heat capacity.

mastery.prompt: Before solving an ice-water mixture for positive Tf, check…
mastery.why: A phase budget determines the possible final state.

mastery.prompt: Ignoring a colder container tends to predict Tf…
mastery.why: Some heat warms the omitted container.

marking.point: Average velocity = (4.00 + 14.0)/2 = 9.00 m/s under constant acceleration.

questions.prompt: A trolley begins at +10.0 m/s with constant acceleration −2.00 m/s² for 7.00 s. Find its turning time, final velocity, displacement and total distance.

marking.point: Forward path to turning point is 25.0 m; backward path during the next 2.00 s is 4.00 m.
Total distance is 29.0 m, different from the 21.0 m net displacement.

mastery.why: Initial velocity is zero; acceleration may be nonzero.

mastery.prompt: With v negative and a negative, speed…
mastery.why: The acceleration acts in the same direction as velocity.

mastery.prompt: Area under v versus t gives…
mastery.why: Velocity multiplied by time contributes displacement.

mastery.prompt: Which equation does not contain time?

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 9.80 m/s and returns to release height. Find apex time, maximum height, return time and return velocity. State acceleration at the apex.

marking.point: Acceleration at apex remains −9.80 m/s² despite momentary zero velocity.

questions.prompt: An object is dropped from rest through 31.36 m. Find fall time and impact velocity, and explain the ideal mass-independence of the result.

marking.point: u = 0; s = −31.36 m with up positive.
The model acceleration has magnitude F/m = mg/m = g, independent of object mass.
Air resistance is neglected, so this does not predict identical real falls when drag matters.

mastery.prompt: A rising thrown object after release is…

accelerated upwards by its launch force forever
mastery.why: Free fall describes the force model, not the direction of motion.

mastery.why: Gravity continues to change velocity.

mastery.prompt: A dropped object has initial velocity…
mastery.why: Dropped from rest means u = 0.

mastery.prompt: A landing below release, up positive, has s…
mastery.why: Final minus initial height is negative.

tasks.constants: Assume constant initial speed during the stated reaction time and constant braking deceleration thereafter. Use point-vehicle geometry unless dimensions are supplied.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 24.0 m/s, has reaction time 0.500 s and then brakes at −6.00 m/s². Find reaction distance, braking distance, total stopping distance and time.

marking.point: Braking time = 24.0/6.00 = 4.00 s; total time = 4.50 s.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 20.0 m/s with 1.00 s reaction delay. A boundary is 60.0 m ahead. Find required braking magnitude. If only 4.00 m/s² is available, find speed at the boundary.

marking.point: Reaction distance = 20.0 m, leaving 40.0 m for braking.
At the boundary v = +√80 = +8.94 m/s; it has not stopped.
The positive velocity root matches reaching the boundary before the rest event.

mastery.prompt: Reaction distance in the constant-speed delay model is…
mastery.why: No braking acceleration is applied yet.

mastery.prompt: At fixed braking magnitude, doubling speed changes braking distance by…
mastery.why: It contains u².
They are consecutive intervals.

mastery.prompt: If reaction travel already exceeds available distance…
options: the boundary is reached before braking begins
mastery.why: There is no positive remaining braking space.

tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², SI units and the stated idealisations. Choose a positive direction; retain calculator guard digits.

questions.prompt: A velocity-time graph shows +6.00 m/s from 0 to 1.00 s, then a straight line to −6.00 m/s at 4.00 s. Find reversal time, displacement and total distance.

marking.point: During the sloped segment a = (−6.00 − 6.00)/3.00 = −4.00 m/s².
Zero velocity occurs 1.50 s after the segment begins, at t = 2.50 s.
First rectangle gives +6.00 m; the later positive and negative triangles each have magnitude 4.50 m.
Net displacement = +6.00 m because the two later signed areas cancel.

questions.prompt: A position-time relationship is x = 5.00 − 2.00t, with SI units. Find velocity, positions at 1.00 s and 4.00 s, displacement over that interval and time of crossing the origin.

marking.point: Displacement = −3.00 − 3.00 = −6.00 m; distance is 6.00 m because velocity never reverses.
Crossing the origin does not mean the object stops; its velocity remains −2.00 m/s.

mastery.why: Slope is Δv/Δt.

options: leftward motion under the chosen axis
mastery.why: Velocity sign gives direction.
Position is unchanged.

mastery.prompt: Distance for a reversing graph requires…
mastery.why: The opposite-direction path still adds to total travel.

marking.point: Rising but slowing means downward acceleration: a = −1.25 m/s² with up positive.
Gravitational weight is 784 N, so the scale reading is lower because acceleration is downward.

mastery.why: Zero net force means zero acceleration.
The forces belong to the two interacting objects.

mastery.why: It opposes relative sliding.

Complete four concept checks, review your written work and record an improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concept answers are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², SI units and the stated idealisations. Choose a positive direction; retain calculator guard digits.

questions.prompt: A 4.00 kg cart at +3.00 m/s hits a stationary 2.00 kg cart and they stick. Neglect external impulse. Find final velocity and kinetic-energy loss.

marking.point: Kinetic-energy loss is 6.00 J; energy transfers to other forms rather than being destroyed.

questions.prompt: A 0.200 kg ball changes velocity from −15.0 m/s to +25.0 m/s in 0.0200 s. Find impulse and average net force, then describe the effect of doubling contact time for the same velocity change.

marking.point: For twice the time and the same impulse, average net force halves to +200 N.
The velocity change, not merely the speed change, must be used for the rebound.

mastery.why: Direction reversal must enter v − u.
Internal interactions can be large.

options: transfers kinetic energy to other forms
mastery.why: Momentum can remain conserved while macroscopic kinetic energy decreases.

tasks.focus: Solve starts, speed changes, reversals and unknown-time problems.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both fresh written questions before revealing the marking guide. Explain equation choices and show units, signs and labelled diagrams where useful. Complete the four concept checks, review written working and record an improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use one-dimensional motion and constant acceleration over the specified interval. Set a positive direction and use SI units.

questions.prompt: A cart starts at +4.00 m/s and accelerates at +2.50 m/s² for 4.00 s. Find final velocity and displacement, then check the displacement using average velocity.

marking.point: Average velocity = (4.00 + 14.0)/2 = 9.00 m/s under constant acceleration.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 20.0 m/s with 1.00 s reaction delay. A boundary is 60.0 m ahead. Find required braking magnitude. If only 4.00 m/s² is available, find speed at the boundary.

marking.point: Reaction distance = 20.0 m, leaving 40.0 m for braking.
At the boundary v = +√80 = +8.94 m/s; it has not stopped.
The positive velocity root matches reaching the boundary before the rest event.

mastery.why: Initial velocity is zero; acceleration may be nonzero.

mastery.prompt: With v negative and a negative, speed…
mastery.why: The acceleration acts in the same direction as velocity.

mastery.prompt: Reaction distance in the constant-speed delay model is…
mastery.why: No braking acceleration is applied yet.

mastery.prompt: At fixed braking magnitude, doubling speed changes braking distance by…
mastery.why: It contains u².

questions.prompt: A ⁶³₂₉Cu nucleus forms a Cu²⁺ ion. State all three particle counts and its net charge.
An equation proposes p → n + e⁻ + νₑ. Use electric charge to explain why it cannot represent beta-plus decay.

marking.point: Beta-plus uses e⁺ and νₑ; a nuclear energy balance must also permit the transformation.

mastery.prompt: A neutral ¹⁴₆C atom has how many electrons?
mastery.why: Electron count equals proton count for a neutral atom.

mastery.prompt: Which change forms a positive ion?
mastery.why: Removing negative electrons leaves net positive charge.
A neutron becomes a proton through d → u.

tasks.constants: Original exam-style questions. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 u c² = 931.5 MeV and 1 MeV = 1.60218 × 10⁻¹³ J when needed; use all supplied masses consistently. Quality factors are supplied exercise values, not universal safety thresholds.

questions.prompt: Distinguish irradiation from contamination using a person exposed to a sealed gamma source and a person with radioactive dust on clothing.

marking.point: Dust is radioactive material present, so contamination.
Removing the sealed source stops that exposure.
Dust can continue emitting until appropriately removed or decayed.

questions.prompt: Explain why time, distance and external shielding alone cannot fully control a radioactive powder inhalation hazard.

marking.point: Inhaled material becomes an internal source.
Its irradiation continues near tissue independently of distance to the original container.
Activity, emitted energy and deposited dose still require assessment.

mastery.why: Two protons plus two neutrons form an alpha.

mastery.prompt: Gamma is deflected by an electric field?
mastery.why: Photons have no electric charge.

mastery.prompt: Doubling ideal point-source distance changes intensity by…
mastery.why: Sphere area is proportional to r².
Transmission is 1 − 0.90.

questions.prompt: A resistor draws 25.0 mA at 5.00 V. Find R and voltage required for 40.0 mA at constant temperature.
A 200 Ω resistor is specified for at most 0.500 W. In an ideal calculation find maximum voltage and current at that limit.

marking.point: At fixed branch voltage, I = V/R means lower resistance gives greater current.
I = 0.0500 A; this is a mathematical rating limit, not installation advice.

options: at an operating point even for non-ohmic components
mastery.why: It defines operating-point resistance.
With voltage vertical and current horizontal, ΔV/ΔI gives resistance in ohms.

mastery.prompt: At fixed I, lead heating depends on…
mastery.why: Resistor heating is P = I²R: square the current, then multiply by resistance.

mastery.prompt: R = ρL/A is labelled here as…
mastery.why: The syllabus core names resistance and circuit relationships rather than resistivity.

tasks.constants: Water c = 4180 J/(kg·K) unless stated. No phase change in Q = mcΔT calculations. Values supplied in each question override these defaults.

questions.prompt: A 0.400 kg water sample warms from 20.0°C to 70.0°C using a 1000 W input heater at 80.0% efficiency. Find useful heating energy, input energy and heating time.

marking.point: No phase change is assumed and efficiency accounts for input not reaching useful water heating.

questions.prompt: A net 300 W heater melts 0.150 kg ice already at 0°C. Use Lf = 334000 J/kg. Find the plateau duration and explain why temperature remains level.

marking.point: Energy changes particle arrangement and interaction energy.
Ice and liquid coexist during melting rather than warming together above 0°C.

mastery.prompt: At fixed mass and ΔT, a larger c requires…
mastery.why: Q = mcΔT.
Offsets cancel in differences.

mastery.prompt: During partial melting of pure ice at standard pressure, temperature is approximately…
mastery.why: Energy changes phase proportions while both phases coexist.
Latent heat applies to converted material.

mastery.why: n counts half-wave loops.

mastery.prompt: First overtone of closed-open pipe is…
mastery.why: Only odd harmonics fit.

mastery.prompt: Consecutive resonance lengths at fixed f differ by…

tasks.constants: Use SI units and stated constants. Keep extra digits until final reporting. Thermal examples specify simplified conditions; vector examples use ordinary low-speed mechanics. All questions are original exam-style practice.

questions.prompt: Explain the transfer mechanisms when a hot metal radiator warms a room. Include the radiator surface and the moving room air.

marking.point: Metal transfers energy by conduction within its material.
The surface emits thermal radiation to surrounding surfaces.
Air near the radiator warms, often expands and becomes less dense.
Buoyant circulation transfers energy by natural convection.

questions.prompt: 1.50 g water evaporates with L = 2.40 × 10⁶ J/kg. If energy comes only from 0.150 kg remaining water, c = 4200, find temperature-drop magnitude and state a limitation.

marking.point: Real surroundings/container can supply energy and the model neglects those transfers.

mastery.why: Conduction can occur without bulk material motion.

options: a stationary rigid solid as a current
mastery.why: Convection transports energy through bulk fluid movement.

mastery.prompt: A refrigerator rejects energy equal to…
mastery.why: Both removed energy and work reach the hot side.
The slope gives the direction and rate of temperature change.

questions.prompt: A student walks 75 m east and 25 m west in 50 s. Find distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity.
A walker is 15.0 m west and 8.00 m north of the start. Find the direct return displacement and explain how to check it.

marking.point: Adding outgoing and return components gives zero net displacement.

mastery.why: Distance sums path lengths without direction.

mastery.prompt: With east positive, 3 m west is…
mastery.why: The sign encodes direction on the defined axis.

options: final speed minus initial speed always
mastery.why: Subtract signed vectors in the definition order.
The opposite has equal magnitude and reversed direction.
